activity: Faxian's starting point. Deploring the imperfect state of the Chinese collection of the Books of Discipline (Vinaya), in 399 CE he and four companions set out for India to seek the disciplinary rules.

date.basis: Legge note: the journey began in A.D. 399 (year Ke-hae); the pilgrimage occupied fifteen years to 414.

coordinates.note: Xi'an (Chang'an), Shaanxi, China.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Ch’ang-gan is the principal district of Se-gan (Xi'an), Shen-se; capital of the Han and of the Ts’in kingdom. No lat/lon given in the note.

source.quote: they should go to India and seek for the Disciplinary Rules.

activity: The pilgrims passed through Lung and stopped here for the summer retreat.

date.basis: First summer retreat after leaving Chang'an in 399.

coordinates.note: Lanzhou region, Gansu (uncertain).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: K’een-kwei was the second king of the Western Ts’in; Faxian found him at his capital somewhere in the present department of Lan-chow (Lanzhou), Kan-suh.

source.quote: where they stopped for the summer retreat.

activity: The pilgrims went forward to this kingdom, then crossed the mountain of Yang-low.

date.basis: Second year of the journey; Legge places the pilgrims at this stage around A.D. 400.

coordinates.note: Southern Liang (Wuwei region), Gansu (uncertain).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the Now-t’an of the text was ruler of the 'southern Leang' from 402; the name Leang remains in Leang-chow (Liangzhou), northern Kan-suh.

source.quote: they went forward to the kingdom of Now-t’an,

activity: Found the country so disturbed that the roads were impassable. The king detained the pilgrims and acted as their danapati (patron). Here they met Pao-yun and other monks bound on the same journey and passed the summer retreat together.

date.basis: Legge: the second summer of the journey, probably A.D. 400.

coordinates.note: Zhangye, Gansu, China.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Chang-yih is still a district in Kan-chow (Zhangye) department, Kan-suh, not far from the Great Wall.

source.quote: reached the emporium of Chang-yih.

activity: Frontier town on the edge of the Gobi. The prefect Le Hao supplied the means of crossing the desert. Faxian and four friends started first, ahead of Pao-yun's party, then traversed the Sandy Desert, where there are evil demons and hot winds, and the only road-marks are the dry bones of the dead.

anecdotes.title: The Sea of Sand
anecdotes.summary: The great desert (Gobi) has no bird in the air nor animal on the ground; travellers find their way only by the dry bones of those who perished before them.

date.basis: Legge places the pilgrims here around A.D. 400, the second year of travel.

coordinates.note: Legge: lat 39°40'N, lon 94°50'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the most western prefecture of Kan-suh, beyond the end of the Great Wall.

source.quote: had supplied them with the means of crossing the desert

activity: Reached after seventeen days (~1500 le) across the desert. A rugged, barren land; the king professed Buddhism. The monks all studied the Lesser Vehicle. Faxian observed that the people and monks here practise the rules of India, and that this held for all the kingdoms westward, each with its own barbarous speech.

date.basis: Reached shortly after the Gobi crossing of c. 400.

coordinates.note: Shanshan/Loulan (Charklik/Ruoqiang region), Xinjiang (uncertain).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Wylie): the capital was not far from Lob (Lop) Nor, south of the lake; Faxian estimated 1500 le from Dunhuang.

source.quote: who were all students of the hinayana.

activity: Reached after fifteen days' walk north-west. The monks, all students of the Lesser Vehicle, were very strict in their rules, so that monks from Ts'in were unprepared for their regulations. Faxian, helped by Foo Kung-sun, stayed over two months and was rejoined by Pao-yun's party. The people then treated the strangers niggardly; some companions turned back, but Faxian's group pressed on south-west.

date.basis: Sequential travel after Shen-shen (c. 400).

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): Karashahr region, Tarim basin. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Watters): not identified; probably in or near Kharaschar (Karashahr), between it and Kutscha (Kucha).

source.quote: In this also there were more than four thousand monks, all

monasteries.text: four great monasteries, not counting the smaller ones

activity: A prosperous kingdom where all profess Buddhism, most monks studying the Great Vehicle. The lord of the country lodged Faxian's party in the Gomati monastery (3000 Mahāyāna monks). Faxian remained three months to see the great procession of images. He describes the King's New Monastery, eighty years in the building.

anecdotes.title: Procession of images
anecdotes.summary: For a fortnight from the first of the fourth month, each monastery in turn drew a towering four-wheeled image-car into the city; the king put off his crown, went barefoot to meet the image, and did homage, while the queen scattered flowers from the gate-tower.

anecdotes.title: The King's New Monastery
anecdotes.summary: A monastery ~250 cubits high, eighty years and three reigns in the building, overlaid with gold and silver; the kings of the six countries east of the Ts'ung range contribute most of their treasures to it.

date.basis: Sequential travel; reached after the Woo-e stay.

coordinates.note: Legge (after P. Smith): town now called Ilchi, lat 37°N, lon 80°35'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Yu-teen is better known as Khoten; Sanskrit name Kustana.

source.quote: most of whom are students of the Mahāyāna.

activity: Reached after twenty-five days. The king was a strenuous follower of Buddhism with over a thousand monks, mostly of the Great Vehicle. The pilgrims abode fifteen days, then went south.

date.basis: Sequential travel after Khotan.

coordinates.note: Tashkurgan or Yarkand region, southern Tarim (uncertain).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: not identified; Beal suggests Yarkand, Watters favours Tashkurgan in Sirikul. At least ~150 miles from Khotan.

source.quote: a thousand monks, mostly students of the Mahāyāna.

activity: Among the Ts'ung-ling (Onion) mountains; the pilgrims halted here and kept their retreat before going on twenty-five days through the hills.

date.basis: Legge: two or three years had elapsed since leaving Chang'an — 'Are we now with them in 402?'

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): Pamir / Tsung-ling (Onion) range. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Watters): not clearly identified; directly south of Tsze-hoh among the Onion mountains, conjecturally Aktasch.

source.quote: where they halted and kept their retreat.

monks.text: more than a thousand monks and their disciples

activity: Reached after twenty-five days through the hills, rejoining Hwuy-king. The king was holding the pancha parishad, the great quinquennial assembly of monks. The country has a stone spittoon and a tooth of Buddha, over which a tope was reared; its thousand-plus monks all studied the Lesser Vehicle.

anecdotes.title: The great quinquennial assembly
anecdotes.summary: The king summons monks from all quarters, decorates the place of session, and presents lavish offerings; he then gives away his horse, woollen cloth and treasures to the monks, and afterwards redeems them.

date.basis: Sequential with the Onion-mountain retreat of c. 402.

coordinates.note: Skardu region, upper Indus (uncertain).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Klaproth/Watters): probably Iskardu/Skardo, which would bring the pilgrims across the Indus; identification uncertain.

source.quote: It happened that the king of the country was then holding the pancha parishad,

activity: The first small kingdom of North India, reached after a month crossing the Onion (Snowy) mountains, whose venomous dragons spit poisonous winds. Many monks, all of the Lesser Vehicle.

anecdotes.title: The wooden image of Maitreya
anecdotes.summary: An Arhat carried a clever artificer up to the Tushita heaven three times to behold Maitreya Bodhisattva and carve his likeness in wood; the finished image is eighty cubits high and emits light on fast-days; surrounding kings vie to make offerings to it.

date.basis: Entry into North India after the Onion-mountain crossing of 402.

coordinates.note: Eitel: lat 30°11'N, lon 73°54'E (Legge himself doubts this identification)

scholarlyNotes.notes: Eitel identifies T’o-leih with Darada/Darel on the western bank of the Indus; Legge expresses more than doubt, placing Faxian on the eastern bank here.

source.quote: where also there were many monks, all students of the hinayana.

activity: After fifteen days south-west along a precipitous range, the pilgrims crossed the Indus by a path of 700 chiselled ladders down the rock face to a rope suspension-bridge, the banks eighty paces apart. Here monks asked Faxian when Buddhism first went east.

anecdotes.title: When the Law first crossed eastward
anecdotes.summary: Faxian relates the local tradition that, after the Maitreya image was set up (~300 years after Buddha's nirvana), Indian monks first carried sutras and books of discipline across this river — the beginning of the Law's diffusion to the east.

date.basis: Continuation of the North India entry of 402.

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): upper Indus gorge near Skardu. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge quotes Cunningham's description of the Indus gorge from Skardo to Makpou-i-shang-rong, spanned by frail rope bridges and rock ladders.

source.quote: the waters of the river called the Indus.

monasteries.text: of these there are in all 500

activity: A flourishing part of North India where the people use the language of Central India. There are 500 sangharamas, the monks all of the Lesser Vehicle; arriving strangers are given three days' supply. Faxian's party kept the summer retreat here, then went south to Soo-ho-to.

anecdotes.title: Buddha's traces in Udyana
anecdotes.summary: Tradition holds Buddha came here, leaving a footprint that appears long or short to each beholder, the rock where he dried his clothes, and the place where he converted the wicked dragon (naga) Apatala.

features: rock where Buddha dried his clothes

date.basis: Legge: 'We would seem now to be in 403' (summer retreat at Woo-chang).

coordinates.note: Swat valley (Mingora region), Pakistan. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Eitel): Udyâna ('the Park'), just north of the Punjab, along the Subhavastu (Swat) river.

source.quote: of these there are in all 500, the monks being all students of the hinayana.

activity: A country where Buddhism is flourishing, reached by descending south from Udyana.

anecdotes.title: The ransom of the dove
anecdotes.summary: Here, in a former age, Sakra tested the Bodhisattva by sending a hawk after a dove; the Bodhisattva cut off a piece of his own flesh to ransom the dove. A tope adorned with gold and silver plates marks the spot.

date.basis: Descended from Udyana after the 403 summer retreat.

scholarlyNotes.modernName: between the Indus and the Swat (uncertain)

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): hill country between the Indus and the Swat. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: not clearly identified; must have been between the Indus and the Swat — 'Swastene'.

source.quote: cut off a piece of his own flesh, and (with it) ransomed the dove.

activity: Reached by going east five days; the land ruled by Dharma-vivardhana, son of Asoka. The people were mostly of the Lesser Vehicle.

anecdotes.title: Buddha gives his eyes
anecdotes.summary: When Buddha was a Bodhisattva he gave away his eyes for another man here; a large tope adorned with gold and silver plates marks the place.

date.basis: Sequential travel within North India in 403.

coordinates.note: Gandhara (Charsadda/Peshawar plain), Pakistan.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Eitel): an ancient kingdom corresponding to the region about Dheri and Banjour.

source.quote: the place where Dharma-vivardhana,(2) the son of Asoka,(3) ruled.

activity: Reached after seven days east. The name means 'the severed head'. Two of the four great topes lie here and nearby; kings, ministers and peoples vie in making offerings, and pilgrims come endlessly to scatter flowers and light lamps.

anecdotes.title: Buddha gives away his head
anecdotes.summary: Here, as a Bodhisattva, Buddha gave away his head to a man, whence the kingdom's name. Two days further east is the place where he threw down his body to feed a starving tigress; large topes mark both.

date.basis: Sequential travel within North India in 403.

coordinates.note: Taxila (Shahdheri), Pakistan. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Cunningham identifies the ruins of Shahdheri (between Indus and Jhelum) as Arrian's Taxila, but Legge argues Faxian's Takshasila lay west of the Indus, between the river and Gandhara.

source.quote: he gave away his head to a man;(2) and from this circumstance the kingdom got its name.

activity: Reached four days south of Gandhara. Faxian saw Kanishka's great tope and Buddha's alms-bowl, guarded by more than seven hundred monks. Here Pao-yun and Sang-king turned back; Hwuy-ying (Hwuy-king) died at the alms-bowl monastery, and Faxian went on alone toward Buddha's skull-bone.

anecdotes.title: King Kanishka's great tope
anecdotes.summary: Buddha foretold to Ananda that a king named Kanishka would build a tope here; Sakra disguised as a herd-boy began one, and Kanishka raised over it a tope more than 400 cubits high — said to be the finest in Jambudvipa.

anecdotes.title: Buddha's alms-bowl
anecdotes.summary: A king of Yueh-she tried to carry off Buddha's alms-bowl, but elephants could not move it; he built a tope and monastery and left a guard. The bowl holds about two pecks, is many-coloured, and fills with a few flowers from the poor yet not with myriads from the rich.

date.basis: Sequential travel within North India in 403.

coordinates.note: Legge: lat 34°8'N, lon 71°30'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge identifies Purushapura with modern Peshawur, the ancient capital of Gandhara.

source.quote: There may be there more than seven hundred monks.

activity: At the city He-lo on the borders of Nagara, Faxian saw the flat-bone of Buddha's skull, guarded under eight seals and daily worshipped by the king. Going north he reached the capital of Nagara (tooth tope, Dipankara offering), Buddha's pewter staff, his Sanghali robe, and the rock-cavern holding Buddha's shadow. By the model tope is a monastery of more than seven hundred monks.

anecdotes.title: The festival of Buddha's skull-bone
anecdotes.summary: Eight men of the great families, each with a seal, open the shrine daily; the skull-bone is set on a jewelled platform, and the king and Vaisya chiefs make offerings before attending to government.

anecdotes.title: Buddha's shadow
anecdotes.summary: In a rock-cavern facing south-west Buddha left his shadow; from ten paces it shows his golden form clearly, but fades as one approaches. No artist sent by the surrounding kings has been able to copy it.

date.basis: Faxian wintered here ('stayed there till the third month of winter') before crossing the Little Snowy Mountains.

coordinates.note: Hidda/Jalalabad (Nagarahara), Afghanistan. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: He-lo is the present Hidda, west of Peshawur and five miles south of Jellalabad; Nagara (Na-k’eeh) lay on the southern bank of the Cabul river ~30 miles west of Jellalabad. No lat/lon given.

source.quote: in the borders of the country of Nagara, where there is the flat-bone of Buddha’s skull,

activity: Crossing southward, the pilgrims met a cold wind on the shaded north side. Hwuy-king, unable to go on, died here; Faxian stroked the corpse and lamented before crossing to the south.

anecdotes.title: Death of Hwuy-king
anecdotes.summary: On the snow-covered northern slope a cold wind made the travellers shiver and lose speech; white froth came from Hwuy-king's mouth and he died, bidding Faxian go on so that they should not all perish.

date.basis: Crossed after wintering at Nagara; the next stop's retreat is dated by Legge to 404.

coordinates.note: Safed Koh range, Afghanistan/Pakistan.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: probably the Safeid Koh, on the way to the Kohat pass.

source.quote: proceeding southwards, crossed the Little Snowy mountains.

activity: Reached on crossing south of the range; nearly three thousand monks, students of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles. The pilgrims kept the summer retreat here.

date.basis: Legge: 'We are now therefore in 404' (summer retreat at Lo-e).

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): eastern Afghanistan (Rohi). Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Lo-e or Rohi is a name for Afghanistan, but only a portion of it can be meant here.

source.quote: where there were nearly three thousand monks, students of both the Mahāyāna and hinayana.

activity: Ten days south of Lo-e; more than three thousand monks, all of the Lesser Vehicle. Three days on, the pilgrims again crossed the Indus, where the country on each side was low and level.

date.basis: Reached after the 404 summer retreat at Lo-e.

coordinates.note: Bannu, Pakistan (Faxian's Poh-na ≈ Xuanzang's Varṇu).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the present district of Bannu, Punjab, between 32°10'–33°15'N and 70°26'–72°E (a range, not a point — coordinates left.).

source.quote: where there are also more than three thousand monks, all students of the hinayana.

activity: After crossing the river, a country where Buddhism was very flourishing and the monks studied both Vehicles. Moved with pity at seeing fellow-disciples from Ts'in, they supplied the pilgrims with what they needed.

date.basis: Sequential travel after Poh-na (404).

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): central Punjab. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Eitel): Bhida — 'the present Punjâb', i.e. a portion of it.

source.quote: where Buddhism was very flourishing, and (the monks) studied both the Mahāyāna and hinayana.

activity: Travelling south-east past many monasteries, the pilgrims reached Mathura on the Jumna, with twenty monasteries and some three thousand monks. From here south is the Middle Kingdom (Central India). Faxian gives a long account of its mild climate, light government, vegetarian customs, the outcast Chandalas, and the regular monastic life — topes to Sariputtra, Maudgalyayana and Ananda, and the offerings of Mahāyāna followers to Prajna-paramita, Manjusri and Kwan-she-yin (Avalokitesvara).

anecdotes.title: Customs of the Middle Kingdom
anecdotes.summary: The people are numerous and happy, need not register households, and use cowries; none kill living creatures, drink liquor, or eat onions and garlic, save the Chandalas, who live apart and strike a piece of wood to warn others of their approach.

features: topes to Sariputtra, Maudgalyayana and Ananda

date.basis: Legge: about six years from Chang'an to Central India (399+6=405).

coordinates.note: Legge (after Hunter): lat 27°30'N, lon 77°43'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Muttra, 'the peacock city', birthplace of Krishna; the P’oo-na river is the Jumna (Yamuna).

source.quote: there were twenty monasteries, which might contain three thousand monks

monks.text: the monks and nuns may be a thousand

activity: Eighteen yojanas south-east. The place where Buddha descended from the Trayastrimsas heaven after preaching to his mother, by three precious flights of steps. Asoka built a vihara and a stone pillar with a lion atop. About a thousand monks and nuns, some of the Greater and some of the Lesser Vehicle, served by a white-eared dragon that secures good harvests. Faxian stayed at the Dragon vihara through the summer retreat.

anecdotes.title: Descent from the Trayastrimsas heaven
anecdotes.summary: As Buddha descended by three jewelled flights of steps, attended by Brahma and Sakra, the nun Utpala, changed into the form of a Chakravartti king, was first to do him reverence. Asoka's men dug to the steps' foot without reaching it; only seven steps remain visible.

date.basis: Within the Central India stay beginning c. 405.

coordinates.note: Legge: lat 27°3'N, lon 79°50'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the name survives in Samkassam, a village 45 miles NW of Canouge.

source.quote: in a kingdom called Sankasya,(1) at the place where Buddha came down

activity: Reached seven yojanas south-east from the Dragon vihara after the summer retreat. The city lies along the Ganges and has two monasteries of the Lesser Vehicle. West of the city, on the northern bank, is the place where Buddha preached on the impermanence of life; a tope marks it.

date.basis: Legge: 'We are now, probably, in 405.'

coordinates.note: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Canouge, on the Ganges; Sanskrit name 'the city of humpbacked maidens'.

source.quote: There are two monasteries in it, the inmates of which are students of the hinayana.

activity: Having crossed the Ganges and gone three yojanas south, the pilgrims reached this village, with topes at the places where Buddha preached, sat, and walked.
features: topes of Buddha's preaching, sitting and walking

date.basis: Sequential with Kanyakubja (405).

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): route corridor between Kanyakubja and Sha-che. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: this village (the Chinese editions read 'forest') has hardly been clearly identified.

source.quote: arrived at a village named A-le,(4) containing places where Buddha preached the Law,

activity: Three yojanas south-east. Outside the south gate is the willow tree that grew from Buddha's discarded tooth-stick, neither increasing nor diminishing at seven cubits; a tope marks where the four Buddhas walked and sat.

anecdotes.title: The tooth-stick willow
anecdotes.summary: Buddha stuck his chewed willow (danta-kashtha) into the ground and it grew to seven cubits; the Brahmans cut and uprooted it in jealousy, but it always grew again on the same spot.

date.basis: Sequential travel within Central India.

coordinates.note: Ayodhya/Saket, Uttar Pradesh (Faxian's Sha-che ≈ Xuanzang's Ayodhyā).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Cunningham): Sha-che (Sha-khe) likely identified with the present Saket.

source.quote: they came to the great kingdom of Sha-che.

activity: Eight yojanas south, the city of Sravasti in Kosala, where king Prasenajit ruled — now reduced to a few more than two hundred families. Faxian and Tao-ching visited the Jetavana vihara, where Buddha lived twenty-five years; the resident monks marvelled that men of a border land had come so far for the Law. Around the Jetavana there had been ninety-eight monasteries. Faxian notes the ninety-six erroneous (non-Buddhist) schools of the Middle Kingdom.

anecdotes.title: The first image of Buddha
anecdotes.summary: When Buddha went up to preach to his mother, king Prasenajit had a sandalwood image carved; on Buddha's return it left its seat to meet him — said to be the very first image of Buddha, the pattern for all later ones.

anecdotes.title: Chanchamana's false accusation
anecdotes.summary: A woman of a heterodox sect feigned pregnancy and accused Buddha before the assembly; Sakra's devas, as white mice, gnawed her girdle so the padding fell, and the earth swallowed her alive into hell. Devadatta likewise went down alive into hell here.

date.basis: Sequential travel within the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Sahet-Mahet (Sravasti). Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Cunningham): the ruins called Sahet Mahat, on the south bank of the Rapti, about 58 miles north of Ayodhya. No lat/lon given.

source.quote: came to the city of Sravasti(1) in the kingdom of Kosala,

activity: Fifty le west of Sravasti, the birthplace of Kasyapa Buddha (a predecessor of Sakyamuni); topes mark where he met his father and attained pari-nirvana, and a great tope covers his whole-body relic.

date.basis: Sequential with Sravasti (c. 406).

coordinates.note: Tadwa near Sahet-Mahet, Uttar Pradesh, India (uncertain).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Cunningham): identified with Tadwa, a village nine miles west of Sahet-Mahet (though Kasyapa Buddha's birthplace is generally thought to be Benares).

source.quote: the birthplace of Kasyapa Buddha.

activity: Twelve yojanas south-east of Sravasti, the birthplace of Krakuchanda Buddha; topes mark where he met his father and attained pari-nirvana. Less than a yojana north is the birthplace-town of Kanakamuni Buddha, similarly marked with topes.

date.basis: Sequential travel toward Kapilavastu (c. 406).

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): route corridor between Too-wei and Kapilavastu. Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Na-pei-kea (Nabhiga) is not mentioned elsewhere; Eitel and Hardy give differing birthplaces for this Buddha.

source.quote: the birthplace of Krakuchanda Buddha.

monks.text: only some monks and a score or two of families

activity: Less than a yojana east; a scene of mound and desolation, with neither king nor people, only some monks and a few families. Images of the prince (Sakyamuni) and his mother stand at king Suddhodana's old palace; topes mark the many incidents of Buddha's birth and youth here. On the roads travellers must guard against white elephants and lions.

anecdotes.title: The four fixed places of all Buddhas
anecdotes.summary: Faxian records the four events fixed in the history of every Buddha: attaining perfect Wisdom; turning the wheel of the Law; preaching and confuting error; and descending from the Trayastrimsas heaven after preaching for their mothers.

features: tope where Vaidurya slew the Sakyas

date.basis: Within the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Legge: a short distance NW of Goruckpoor, lat 26°46'N, lon 83°19'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the birthplace of Sakyamuni, destroyed in his lifetime; Davids places it on the river Rohini, ~100 miles NW of Benares.

source.quote: but in it there was neither king nor people.

activity: Fifty le east of Kapilavastu, the garden where queen Maya, holding a tree-branch, gave birth to the heir-apparent (Buddha). A well formed where two dragon-kings washed the newborn, from which the monks still draw water.

anecdotes.title: The birth of the Buddha
anecdotes.summary: Coming forth from the pond, the queen laid hold of a branch and gave birth facing east; the child walked seven paces, and two dragon-kings washed his body, forming a well on the spot.

date.basis: Visited from Kapilavastu (c. 406).

coordinates.note: Lumbini, Nepal. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: The garden of Buddha's birth, 50 le east of Kapilavastu (no lat/lon in Legge's notes).

source.quote: was a garden, named Lumbini,(17) where the queen entered the pond and bathed.

activity: Five yojanas east of Buddha's birthplace; its king had built the Rama tope over one portion of Buddha's relics, watched over by a dragon. A devotee, moved that elephants tended the neglected tope, resumed the status of a Sramanera and founded a monastery; ever since there has been a Sramanera head of the establishment.

anecdotes.title: The dragon that guarded the relics
anecdotes.summary: When Asoka sought to open the eight relic-topes to build 84,000, the dragon of the Rama tope showed him its peerless offerings; unable to surpass them, Asoka left this tope alone. Afterwards a herd of elephants watered and tended the overgrown tope until a devotee built a monastery there.

date.basis: Sequential travel toward Kusinagara.

coordinates.note: Ramagrama stupa, Nepal terai (approximate).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Rama or Ramagrama, between Kapilavastu and Kusanagara.

source.quote: there is a kingdom called Rama.(1)

monks.text: only the families belonging to the societies of monks

activity: Reached by way of the Charcoal tope (cremation site) and the place where the prince sent back Chandaka and his white horse. North of the city, between two sala trees on the Nairanjana's bank, is where Buddha attained pari-nirvana (died). Topes and monasteries mark where Subhadra was converted, the body lay in state, and the eight kings divided the relics. The city is nearly empty.

anecdotes.title: Buddha's pari-nirvana and the division of relics
anecdotes.summary: Buddha died here, head to the north, between two trees; Subhadra, his last convert, attained Arhatship; after seven days' offerings the eight kings divided the relics at the suggestion of the brahman Drona.

route.distance: via two stages of 4 yojanas, then 12 yojanas

date.basis: Sequential travel within the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Davids): Kusinara, near Kusiah, ~120 miles NNE of Benares and 80 miles due east of Kapilavastu. No lat/lon given.

source.quote: is the place where the World-honoured one, with his head to the north, attained to pari-nirvâna (and died).

activity: Ten yojanas east. North of the city is the double-galleried vihara where Buddha dwelt and the tope over half of Ananda's body. Ambapali the courtesan built a vihara and gave her garden to Buddha. North-west is the tope 'Bows and weapons laid down', and to the east the tope of the second Great Council, where 700 monks revised the disciplinary books a century after Buddha's death.

anecdotes.title: The Council of Vaisali
anecdotes.summary: A hundred years after Buddha's pari-nirvana, Bhikshus of Vaisali went wrong on ten points of discipline; 700 Arhats and observant monks re-examined and collated the books of discipline (the second Great Council).

anecdotes.title: Bows and weapons laid down
anecdotes.summary: A king's discarded son, set adrift in a box, fathered a thousand mighty sons who came to attack their grandfather's kingdom; their true mother revealed herself from the wall, sending jets of milk into their mouths, and they laid down their weapons — the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadra-kalpa.

date.basis: Sequential travel toward Magadha within the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Basarh (Vaishali), Bihar. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the ruins still exist at Bassahar/Besarh, north of Patna, ~20 miles north of Hajipur.

source.quote: having in it the double-galleried vihâra(1) where Buddha dwelt,

names.asGiven: the confluence of the five rivers

activity: Four yojanas east; the river where Ananda attained pari-nirvana, dividing his body so that king Ajatasatru and the Lichchhavis each received half as a relic, over which each raised a tope.

anecdotes.title: The death of Ananda
anecdotes.summary: Going from Magadha to Vaisali, Ananda was met on the river by both Ajatasatru's pursuing army and the Lichchhavis coming to meet him; to favour neither, he burned his body mid-stream by the fire of Samadhi and divided the relic between the two banks.

date.basis: Sequential with Vaisali toward Patna.

coordinates.note: The Ganges confluence near Patna (approximate).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: this spot does not appear to have been identified; it could not be far from Patna.

source.quote: the confluence of the five rivers.

activity: The chief city of Magadha and the Middle Kingdom, where Asoka ruled; his spirit-built palace still stands. Beside Asoka's tope are a Mahāyāna monastery and a Śrāvakayāna monastery, together holding six or seven hundred monks. Faxian later returned and stayed three years here, learning Sanskrit and copying the Vinaya — obtaining the Mahasanghika rules (from the Jetavana tradition) and a transcript of the Sarvāstivāda rules, plus several other texts. Vaisya elders run free dispensaries and hospitals for the poor and sick.

anecdotes.title: Asoka's gift of Jambudvipa
anecdotes.summary: A stone pillar before Asoka's great tope bears the inscription that Asoka gave Jambudvipa to the whole body of monks and three times redeemed it from them with money.

anecdotes.title: Radha-sami, the Mahāyāna Brahman
anecdotes.summary: A Brahman named Radha-sami, a Mahāyāna teacher of clear discernment, was so revered that the king served him as a teacher; through him the Law of Buddha was widely spread and other doctrines could not persecute the monks.

date.basis: Legge: Faxian's stoppages in Central India extended over six years; he stayed three years at Patna learning Sanskrit and copying the Vinaya before going on to Tamalipti.

coordinates.note: Legge: modern Patna, lat 25°28'N, lon 85°15'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: the Sanskrit name means 'the city of flowers'; Asoka transferred his court here from Rajagriha.

source.quote: in the kingdom of Magadha, the city where king Asoka(2) ruled.

activity: Nine yojanas south-east of Patna; a stone apartment facing south where Buddha sat while Sakra, with the deva-musician Pancha-sikha, gave him pleasure on the lute and asked him forty-two questions traced on the rock. A monastery stands here.

anecdotes.title: Sakra's forty-two questions
anecdotes.summary: Sakra brought the deva-musician Pancha-sikha to delight Buddha with the lute, then asked Buddha forty-two questions, tracing each with his finger on the rock; the prints are still there.

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Indrasailaguha (Giryek), Bihar (usual identification).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Xuanzang): Indra-sila-guha, 'the cavern of Indra', a hill near Giryek on the Panchana river, ~36 miles from Gaya.

source.quote: Sakra then asked Buddha about forty-two subjects, tracing (the questions) out with his finger one by one on the rock.

activity: A yojana south-west of the rocky hill, the village of Nala (Nalanda), birthplace of Sariputtra, to which he returned and attained pari-nirvana; a tope was built over the place where his body was burned.

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Nalanda Mahavihara ruins, Bargaon. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Nala or Nalanda, identified with the present Baragong; a grand monastery was later built here, famous for Xuanzang's five-year residence.

source.quote: brought them to the village of Nala,(5) where Sariputtra(6) was born,

activity: A yojana west, New Rajagriha, built by king Ajatasatru, with two monasteries and his relic-tope outside the west gate. South lies the old city of Bimbisara within a ring of five hills; here Sariputtra and Maudgalyayana met Upasena, the Nirgrantha laid his fire-pit, Ajatasatru loosed a drunk elephant against Buddha, and Jivaka built a vihara — but inside the old city all is now emptiness and desolation.

anecdotes.title: The drunk elephant
anecdotes.summary: At the prompting of Devadatta, king Ajatasatru made a black elephant drunk with liquor and loosed it to injure Buddha; the elephant instead did homage to him.

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Rajgir (old Rajagriha), Bihar. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Eitel): the residence of the Magadha kings from Bimbisara to Asoka; ruins at the village of Rajghir, 16 miles SW of Behar. New Rajagriha distinguished from old Kusagarapura.

source.quote: the new city which was built by king Ajatasatru.

activity: The highest of the five hills, with Buddha's meditation cave, Ananda's cave, and the cliff from which Devadatta threw a rock at Buddha's toes. Faxian bought incense, flowers, oil and lamps in the New City and, with two resident monks, climbed the peak; he made his offerings, lit the lamps at dusk, wept that he had been born too late to meet Buddha, chanted the Surangama Sutra, and passed the night on the peak.

anecdotes.title: Faxian's night on the Vulture Peak
anecdotes.summary: Overcome with melancholy, Faxian declared, 'Here Buddha delivered the Surangama Sutra. I, Fa-hien, was born when I could not meet with Buddha,' chanted the Sutra before the rock cavern, and stayed there overnight — one of the most personal moments of his record.

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Griddhakuta (Vulture Peak) hill, Rajgir. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: 'The Hill of the Vulture Cavern', the highest of the five hills around Rajagriha.

source.quote: came to mount Gridhra-kuta.

activity: On the north of the hill, the cave where 500 Arhats collected the Sutras after Buddha's nirvana (the first Great Council), with Mahakasyapa presiding and Ananda shut outside the door. Nearby are the Karanda Bamboo garden (Venuvana) with its old vihara, the Pippala cave where Buddha meditated after his meal, and the black rock where a bhikshu took his own life and attained Arhatship.

anecdotes.title: The First Council
anecdotes.summary: After Buddha's nirvana, 500 Arhats gathered here to collect the Sutras; Sariputtra and Maudgalyayana's seats on left and right, Mahakasyapa president in the middle, and Ananda — one short of the five hundred — could not get in.

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Rajgir (old Rajagriha), Bihar. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: a very great place in Buddhist annals; the cave was prepared by king Ajatasatru for the first synod.

source.quote: the place where, after the nirvâna(5) of Buddha, 500 Arhats collected the Sûtras.

variants: Gaya and the Bodhi tree (Bodh Gaya)

activity: Four yojanas west; the city of Gaya is empty and desolate, but south of it lie the great sites of Buddha's enlightenment: the place of his six years' austerities, the Gramika girls' rice-gruel offering, and the patra (Bodhi) tree where, seated facing east on the kusa grass, he overcame Mara and attained perfect Wisdom. Three monasteries stand at the enlightenment place, their monks strict in discipline and well supplied. This is the second of the four great topes (where Buddha attained Wisdom).

anecdotes.title: The defeat of Mara
anecdotes.summary: Mara sent three beautiful women and his demon-soldiers to tempt and assail the Bodhisattva; when he put his toes to the ground the soldiers dispersed and the women were changed into old grandmothers, and he attained Buddhahood.

anecdotes.title: King Asoka and the Bodhi tree
anecdotes.summary: Asoka, who in a former birth had given Buddha a handful of earth and so became a wheel-king, repented his cruel 'naraka' (private hell) under this tree. When his queen had the tree cut down, he poured a hundred pitchers of cows' milk on the stump and vowed not to rise till it lived; it grew again, now nearly 100 cubits high.

features: place of the six years' austerities

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Legge: Gaya was NW of the present Gayah, lat 24°47'N, lon 85°1'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: Gaya, a city of Magadha; Sakyamuni lived here seven years until he attained Buddhaship. The enlightenment site is modern Bodh Gaya.

source.quote: came to the city of Gaya;(1) but inside the city all was emptiness and desolation.

activity: Three le south; the mountain inside which the complete body of Kasyapa (the disciple Mahakasyapa) abides. Devotees from many countries come yearly to offer to Kasyapa, and to the strong in faith Arhats come by night to resolve their doubts. The hill has many lions, tigers and wolves.

anecdotes.title: Mahakasyapa within the mountain
anecdotes.summary: Mahakasyapa made a cleft and went down into the mountain; his complete body still abides in a recess, and the earth with which he washed his hands cures sores on the head of those who plaster it on.

route.fromPlace: Gaya and the Bodhi tree (Bodh Gaya)

date.basis: Excursion in Magadha during the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Gurpa/Kurkihar hill east of Bodh Gaya (usual identification).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge (after Eitel): 'Fowl's-foot hill', with three peaks resembling a chicken's foot, ~7 miles SE of Gaya.

source.quote: came to a mountain named Gurupada,(1) inside which Mahakasyapa even now is.

activity: Returning toward Patna along the Ganges, then twelve yojanas to Varanasi in Kasi. North-east of the city is the vihara in the Deer Park (Sarnath), where Buddha first turned the wheel of the Law, converting Kaundinya and his four companions, and where the dragon Elapattra questioned him. Two monasteries with resident monks.

anecdotes.title: The first turning of the wheel of the Law
anecdotes.summary: In the Deer Park Buddha first preached, converting Kaundinya and his four former companions who had doubted him after his austerities; topes mark where they rose to salute him and where he delivered his prophecy concerning Maitreya.

date.basis: On the way back westward toward Patna, near the end of the Central India stay.

coordinates.note: Legge: modern Benares, lat 25°23'N, lon 83°5'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: 'the city surrounded by rivers'; the Deer Park is modern Sarnath.

source.quote: at the city of Varanasi(3) in the kingdom of Kasi.

monks.text: most of whom are students of the hinayana

activity: Thirteen yojanas north-west of the Deer Park; its Ghochiravana vihara, where Buddha formerly resided, has a company of monks mostly of the Lesser Vehicle. Eight yojanas east is the place where Buddha converted an evil demon, with a monastery of more than a hundred monks.

date.basis: Near the end of the Central India stay, before returning to Patna.

coordinates.note: Legge: identified by some with Kusia near Kurrah (lat 25°41'N, lon 81°27'E), by others with Kosam on the Jumna

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: two competing identifications; Kosam on the Jumna, ~30 miles above Allahabad, is the more common.

source.quote: there is a kingdom named Kausambi.(12)

activity: Reported, not visited. Two hundred yojanas south lies Dakshina, where a five-storey monastery dedicated to Kasyapa Buddha is hewn from a single hill of rock — its tiers shaped as elephant, lion, horse, ox and pigeon, with a spring winding down through the cells. Called Paravata ('pigeon'); Arhats reside there. Faxian gives the account only from men of the country, being unable to go.

anecdotes.title: The Pigeon Monastery
anecdotes.summary: The rock-hewn monastery's five storeys (1500 cells in all) descend in the forms of five animals; villagers say winged men come and enter it, and once told visiting devotees 'Why do you not fly?' — to which the strangers answered that their wings were not yet fully formed.

date.basis: No date: Faxian did not visit Dakshina; he narrates it from hearsay, so no point in his itinerary applies.

coordinates.note: Approximate region centroid (low confidence): the Deccan (reported, not visited). Not a precise identification.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: said to be the ancient name of the Deccan; the chapter is given only from hearsay, and the description differs from Xuanzang's.

source.quote: there is a country named Dakshina,(1) where there is a monastery

activity: Eighteen yojanas east down the Ganges, on the southern bank; topes mark where Buddha walked in meditation by his vihara and where he and his three predecessor Buddhas sat, all with resident monks.
features: topes of Buddha and his predecessors

date.basis: On the eastward journey down the Ganges toward Tamalipti, near the end of the India sojourn.

coordinates.note: Champanagar near Bhagalpur, Bihar. Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: probably Champanagur, 3 miles west of Baglipoor (Bhagalpur); his note gives lat 25°14'N but a longitude of 56°55'E, evidently a misprint (Bhagalpur is near 87°E). Coordinates left.

source.quote: the great kingdom of Champa,(1)

activity: A seaport with twenty-two monasteries and flourishing Buddhism. Faxian stayed two years writing out his sutras and drawing images, then embarked on a large merchant-vessel and, with a favourable winter wind, sailed fourteen days south-west to Ceylon.

date.basis: Legge: Faxian stayed two years at Tamalipti before sailing for Ceylon; this falls near the end of the ~6-year India stay, before the 3-year return.

coordinates.note: Legge: modern Tam-look, lat 22°17'N, lon 88°2'E

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: then the principal emporium for trade with Ceylon and China, near the mouth of the Hoogly.

source.quote: In the country there are twenty-two monasteries,

activity: A large island reached after fourteen days' sail. Faxian describes the Abhayagiri monastery (5000 monks) with its twenty-cubit jade Buddha, the Bo tree grown from a slip of the patra tree at Buddha Gaya, the great festival of Buddha's tooth, the Maha-vihara (3000 monks), and the Chaitya hill (Mihintale, 2000 monks); some sixty thousand monks in all are fed from common stores. Here, seeing a merchant offer a white silk fan, Faxian was overcome by homesickness and wept. In Ceylon he obtained the Mahisasaka Vinaya and other texts unknown in China.

anecdotes.title: The festival of Buddha's tooth
anecdotes.summary: Each third month the king proclaims Buddha's deeds, lines the road with the five hundred forms of the Bodhisattva's past births, and carries the tooth in procession to the Abhayagiri-vihara, where it is venerated for ninety days before returning to the city.

anecdotes.title: The white silk fan
anecdotes.summary: Years from home, with companions dead or scattered, Faxian saw a merchant offer a fan of white silk beside the jade image and the tears of sorrow involuntarily filled his eyes.

anecdotes.title: Cremation of an Arhat
anecdotes.summary: Faxian witnessed (too late to see him alive) the cremation of a Sramana reputed an Arhat at the Maha-vihara, and the king's golden-plough endowment of a new vihara, the grant engraved on plates of metal.

date.basis: Legge: the return took three years from leaving India (c. 411) to reaching Ts'ing-chow (414); Faxian stayed two years in Ceylon, then five months at Java, then sailed for China.

coordinates.note: Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka (the ancient capital). Standard scholarly identification; coordinates of the known site/city.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: 'the Kingdom of the Lion', Ceylon. The Abhayagiri and Maha-vihara monasteries and Mihintale lie at/near Anuradhapura. No lat/lon in the notes.

source.quote: they came to the country of Singhala.(4)

activity: After a stormy ninety-day sea passage from Ceylon, Faxian reached Java-dvipa, where Brahmanism and other forms of error flourished while Buddhism was negligible. He stayed five months, then embarked on another large merchantman bound north-east for Kwang-chow (Canton).

anecdotes.title: Cast adrift in the storm
anecdotes.summary: On the voyage out, a leak forced the merchants to throw goods overboard; Faxian cast away his pitcher and basin but, fearing for his books and images, fixed his heart on Kwan-she-yin (Avalokitesvara) until the ship reached an island and was repaired.

date.basis: On the return voyage; reached after ~90 days from Ceylon, stayed five months, then sailed for China in 413–414.

coordinates.note: Java/Sumatra, Indonesia (identification debated).

scholarlyNotes.notes: Java-dvipa; exact island debated by scholars. No coordinates in Legge's notes.

source.quote: they arrived at a country called Java-dvipa, where various forms of error and Brahmanism are flourishing, while Buddhism in it is not worth speaking of.

activity: After a second storm-tossed passage of more than seventy days, the ship at last reached the China coast south of Mount Lao, on the border of the Ch'ang-kwang prefecture (Shandong). The Buddhist prefect Le E met Faxian and received his books and images. After a winter and summer he went south to the Capital (Nanking) and exhibited the Sutras and Vinaya he had brought. His travels had occupied about fifteen years.

anecdotes.title: Brahmans blame the monk
anecdotes.summary: When a black storm struck, the Brahmans on board resolved to maroon Faxian as the cause of their misfortune; a patron threatened to denounce them to the king of Han, and they did not dare. The provisions nearly gone, the ship turned north-west and reached China.

date.basis: Legge: Faxian reached Ts'ing-chow on his return; the record's envoy dates the meeting to the year Keah-yin (A.D. 414), fifteen years after his 399 departure.

coordinates.note: Mount Lao (Laoshan) near Qingdao, Shandong, China.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Legge: south of the Shantung promontory, at the foot of Mount Lao; the district was later renamed Ch'ang-kwang. The 'Capital' he then went to was Nan-king.

source.quote: they reached the shore on the south of mount Lao,(8) on the borders of the prefecture of Ch’ang-kwang,
